This petition under Section 166 MV act is filed by the Petitioner seeking compensation of Rs.10,00,000/- for the injuries sustained by him in a road traffic accident.

2. It is the specific case of the petitioner that on 02.04.2022 at about 1.40 p.m., he was riding his motorcycle bearing registration No. KA-01-JM-2771 on Outer Ring Road near J.P. Morgan,
Bengaluru.
At that time, the driver of the Tata Ace bearing registration No. KA-01-AB-6485 (hereinafter referred to as the "offending vehicle") drove the same in a rash and negligent manner.

It is alleged that the driver of the offending vehicle first dashed against a car bearing registration No.
KA-53-A-8664 from behind, and thereafter, without giving any signal, suddenly took a right turn and dashed against the petitioner's motorcycle.
3. Due to the impact, the petitioner fell down and sustained grievous injuries.
Immediately after the accident, he was shifted to Yashomathi Hospital, where he took treatment as an inpatient and also underwent surgery.
At the time of the accident, the petitioner was working as a delivery boy with Swiggy and was earning a sum of Rs. 25,000/- per month.
It is his case that on account of the injuries sustained, he has lost his earning capacity and income.
The petitioner has further asserted that he spent about Rs. 1,50,000/- towards medical expenses, conveyance, food, nourishment, and other incidental charges during his treatment.

On these grounds, the petitioner has sought compensation from Respondent Nos. 1 to 4, being the owner, driver, and insurer of the offending vehicle, for the injuries, permanent disability, loss of income, and expenses incurred by him..
Kumar.

sentences.text: In response to the petition notice, the Respondent No.2 and 4 have appeared before the court through the counsel and filed the written statements.
The respondent No.1 and 3 have not appeared and they were placed exparte.
5. Respondent No. 2 has filed its written statement denying the averments of the petitioner.
It has specifically contended that it has not issued any insurance policy in respect of the offending vehicle and therefore, it is not the insurer of the said vehicle.
It is further contended that the accident was not caused due to rash and negligent driving of the offending vehicle, but solely due to the negligence of the petitioner himself.

Respondent No. 2 has also denied the nature of injuries,
occupation, income of the petitioner, treatment expenses, and the extent of liability.
It has further contended that the compensation claimed is excessive and exaggerated.

On these grounds,
Respondent No. 2 has prayed for dismissal of the petition against it.
6. Respondent No. 4 has also filed its written statement, denying all the averments of the petition.
It has contended that this respondent is neither a necessary nor proper party for adjudication of the present case.

Respondent No. 4 has further contended that the vehicle in question is a commercial Tata Ace vehicle, but Respondent No. 1, while obtaining the policy, misrepresented the facts by declaring that the insured vehicle was a Honda Activa two-wheeler bearing No. KA-01-AB-6485, and accordingly paid a premium of only Rs. 887/- (inclusive of tax) for a liability-only, private bike policy.
7. This respondent has never issued a policy for the offending vehicle (Tata Ace).
It is further stated that Respondent No. 1 obtained the said policy by suppression and misrepresentation of material facts, in order to evade payment of the actual premium as per IRDAI norms.
Upon discovery of this fraudulent act, Respondent No. 4 cancelled the policy from its inception for misrepresentation, after due intimation by way of email communication and SMS.
On these grounds, Respondent No. 4 has also prayed for dismissal of the petition against it.

8. On the basis of the above pleadings, the following Issues were framed :-
1.

Whether the Petitioner proves that he sustained injuries when he was riding motorcycle bearing no.KA-01-JM-2771 on 02-04-2022, about 1.45 p.m., Outer Ring Road, near JP Morgan, Kadubisanahalli, Bengaluru District, only due to rash and negligent driving of the driver of Tata Ace bearing No.KA-01-AB-6485?

2. What compensation petitioner is entitled?
3. What order?
9. In order to prove the claim, the Petitioner examined himself as PW.1, doctor is examined as PW-2 and got marked the documents as per Ex.P.1 to P.13.

On the other hand, the Respondent No. 4 has examined its Senior Manager as RW.1 and got marked the documents at Ex.R1 to 7.
10.
I heard the counsel on both sides and have perused the material on record.
Kumar.

By considering the available materials on record and the arguments addressed by the parties, I have answered the above Issues as under:
Issue No.1: In the Affirmative.
Issue No.2: Partly in affirmative.
Issue No.3: As per the final order, for the following:

REASONS 12. ISSUE NO.1:- It is case of the petitioner that on 02.04.2022 at about 1.40 p.m., he was riding his motorcycle bearing registration No. KA-01-JM-2771 on Outer Ring Road near J.P. Morgan,
Bengaluru.
At that time, the driver of the offending vehicle drove the same in a rash and negligent manner.

It is alleged that the driver of the offending vehicle first dashed against a car bearing registration No. KA-53-A-8664 from behind, and thereafter, without giving any signal, suddenly took a right turn and dashed against the petitioner's motorcycle.
Due to the impact, the petitioner fell down and sustained grievous injuries.
13. The petitioner examined himself as PW.1 and reiterated the contents of his claim petition by filing an affidavit in lieu of chief examination under Order XVIII Rule 4 CPC.

In support of his case,
he produced police records at Ex.P1 to Ex.P7, namely FIR, complaint, wound certificate, spot mahazar, spot sketch, IMV report, and charge sheet.

He further examined Dr. B. Ramesh,
Orthopedic Surgeon, as PW.2, who produced Ex.P12 and Ex.P13.

The medical evidence at Ex.P3 - wound certificate - clearly establishes that the petitioner sustained a fracture of the left patella,
which is certified as a grievous injury.
14. Respondent No. 4, in its written statement, has not taken any specific contention disputing the negligence of the offending vehicle.
Its main defence is that respondent No. 1 had obtained the policy by misrepresentation and fraud.
Apart from this, it has generally denied the accident and negligence without placing any material on record.

During the course of cross-examination of PW.1,
learned counsel for respondent No. 4 suggested that the accident occurred solely due to the negligence of the driver of the car in front of the petitioner and also due to the petitioner's own fault.
PW.1 admitted that he was riding his motorcycle near the road divider and that he saw the car at a distance of about 50 meters.
He further deposed that the offending Tata Ace vehicle, which was being driven at an excessive speed, first dashed against the car and thereafter hit him.

The specific suggestion that the accident was caused by his own negligence was critically denied by PW.1.
15.
Nothing substantial was elicited in the cross- examination of PW.1 to discredit his version.
Similarly, the testimony of PW.2, the medical witness, also remained unshaken.

Respondent No. 2,
though arrayed as a party, did not contest the matter after filing its written statement and did not choose to cross- examine the petitioner or lead any rebuttal evidence.
Respondent No. 3 remained ex parte, and respondent No. 1 also did not contest the case.
16. The version of PW.1 is consistent and finds corroboration from the contemporaneous police records, namely FIR, complaint, spot mahazar, spot sketch, IMV report, and charge sheet.
All these documents attribute negligence to the driver of the offending Tata Ace vehicle.
It is a settled Kumar.

4 principle that mere suggestions in cross-examination, unless supported by cogent evidence, cannot form the basis to disbelieve a witness or to shift liability.

In the present case, respondent No. 4 has not produced any independent witness or documentary evidence to substantiate its allegation that the accident was caused due to the negligence of the petitioner or the driver of the car in front of him.

17. Therefore, on a cumulative assessment of oral and documentary evidence, this Tribunal is satisfied that the petitioner sustained injuries in the road traffic accident that occurred on 05.04.2023 due to the rash and negligent driving of the driver of the offending Tata Ace vehicle.
The defence raised by respondent No. 4 remains unsubstantiated and cannot be accepted.
Hence, Issue No.1 is answered in the Affirmative.
18. ISSUE NO.2 :- As per Ex.P.3 wound certificate, the petitioner has sustained comminuted fracture of left patella and Doctor opined that the said injury is grievous in nature.

19. Due to the impact, Petitioner sustained grievous injuries and was shifted to Yashomati Hospital,
wherein he was treated as an inpatient from 02.04.2022 to 06.04.2022.
The petitioner claims that injuries sustained have led to permanent disability, rendering him unable to lead a normal life as earlier.
20. The petitioner examined Dr. Ramesh, Orthopedic Surgeon, Victoria Hospital, who produced Exhibits P-12 and P-13.
PW-2 deposed that the petitioner had sustained a comminuted fracture of the left patella, for which internal fixation was carried out, and subsequently, removal of the implants was also performed.
PW-2 further stated that he clinically and radiologically examined the petitioner for the purpose of disability assessment.
The petitioner complains of difficulties of squat on floor, climb upstairs, walk on slope, kneel.
Based on his evaluation, he assessed that the petitioner had sustained 22% permanent disability in relation to the left lower limb and 11% to the whole body.
21. During the course of cross-examination of PW2, he admitted that a patella fracture usually unites within 4 to 6 weeks.
After removal of suture physiotherapy is commenced.
He further admitted that both wires had been removed from the patella after ensuring union of fracture through an X-ray.
He has also clearly stated that no infection at the fracture site during the course of his examination.

22. It is pertinent to note that although PW-2 assessed 22% disability of the left lower limb and 11%
of the whole body, he did not specifically opine regarding the functional disability, i.e., the actual impact of the disability on the petitioner's earning capacity and day-to-day life.
It is a settled principle that medical disability and functional disability are not always identical.
Functional disability depends on the nature of occupation and the requirement of physical activity for earning livelihood.
As per record the petitioner was employed as a Delivery boy.

Having regard to the nature of the fracture, the subsequent removal of implants, the absence of any further surgical requirement,
and the fact that the petitioner is able to move independently though with certain restrictions, the medical assessment of 22% permanent disability of the limb appears to be on the higher side.
Kumar.

sentences.text: Therefore, while the medical assessment cannot be accepted in its entirety, the tribunal is of the opinion that a fair and reasonable estimate of functional disability of the petitioner, having regard to his avocation, would be taken at 8% of the whole body for the purpose of computing future loss of earning capacity and compensation.
23. In the petition the age of the petitioner is mentioned as 24 years.

Ex.P.10 - Aadhar card of the petitioner shows that he was born on 01-01.998, the same is considered, then age of the petitioner as on the date of accident as 24 years and the multiplier applicable to the case on hand is 18.
24.
At time of the accident, the petitioner was 24 years old and he was working as a delivery boy in Swiggy and earning a sum of Rs.25,000/- per month.
It is asserted that he has lost his earning capacity and income due to accidental injuries.
The petitioner also contends that he incurred significant medical, conveyance, and incidental expenses for his treatment.
However, the petitioner has not produced any documents to substantiate his income.
In the absence of proof of income, this tribunal is of the opinion that the notional income to be assessed as per the guidelines of the Karnataka State Legal Service Authority.

Since the accident has been occurred in the year 2022,
notional income Rs.15,500/- per month is taken for the assessment of compensation.

25. Thus this tribunal is of the opinion that the petitioner who sustained the injuries is entitled for compensation under the following heads:
26. Loss of future income on account of permanent disability:
Considering the petitioner's grievous injury which has resulted in performing daily vocational activities, this court is of the opinion that the functional disability of 8 % is reasonable and just.
27. The petitioner was 24 years old as on date of alleged accident and the multiplier applicable to the petitioner as per decision laid down by Hon'ble Apex court in Sarla Verma's case is at 18.
The notional income taken as Rs.15,500 x 12 x 18 x 8/100= Rs.2,67,840/- towards loss of future income.
28. Pain and sufferings:

So far as the compensation under non-pecuniary damages are concerned,
considering the nature of the injury, which has resulted in difficulty in mobility and in performing daily vocational activities, as well as the duration of inpatient treatment and physical and mental suffering endured by the petitioner, this tribunal is of the opinion that an amount of .40,000/-
would be just and fair compensation under the head pain and sufferings.
29. Loss of amenities of life:
undoubtedly the petitioner is suffering from difficulties in performing day to day activities and is facing continuous hardship due to the disability.
Therefore this tribunal finds to appropriate to award a sum .25,000/- under head of loss of amenities of life.
30. Medical expenses:
Under the pecuniary damages, expenses relating to treatment, hospitalization and medicines, the Petitioner has relied on medical bills at Ex.P.9.

On perusal of these medical bills,
it reveals that the Petitioner has spent .16,255/- towards medical expenses.
The medical bills appears to be genuine.

Therefore, the Petitioner is entitled for medical expenses of .16,255/-
towards Medical Expenses.
Kumar.

Liability:

It is the specific contention of Respondent No. 4 Insurance Company that the insured (Respondent No. 1) committed misrepresentation by obtaining an insurance policy meant for a motorcycle, while in fact the offending vehicle involved in the accident was an Tata ace.
Therefore, it is pleaded that the contract of insurance is void ab initio, and the insurer is not liable to indemnify the insured.
35.On the other hand, the petitioner contends that once a policy is issued by the insurer in respect of a particular vehicle, the insurer cannot escape liability to third-party victims.

It is further urged that it was the bounden duty of the insurer to verify the particulars of the vehicle before issuing the policy, and any lapse or negligence on the part of the insurer cannot prejudice the rights of innocent third-party claimants.

He relied upon the decisions rendered in National Insurance Co. Ltd. v. M.
Nandan and others [2004 ACJ 1449], the Madras High Court clarified that even in cases of fraud or misrepresentation by the insured, the insurer must first satisfy the award.

Robi Kurayekosa [MACA No. 877/2009], the courts recognized that suppression of material facts going to the root of the contract could render the policy void ab initio.

sentences.text: However, those cases were based on clear evidence of deliberate suppression and fraud by the insured.
37. In the present case, respondent No. 4 has not produced any cogent evidence to establish fraudulent intent on the part of the Respondent no 1 in relation to the policy.

The insurer has merely relied upon the discrepancy in the vehicle description, namely that the policy produced relates to a motorcycle, whereas the offending vehicle involved in the accident is a Tata Ace.

This discrepancy,
on the face of it, indicates that some misrepresentation may have been practiced at the time of obtaining the policy.

38. However, the legal position is well settled that the statutory liability of the insurer towards third-party victims under the Motor Vehicles Act cannot be avoided merely on the ground of misrepresentation or fraud practiced by the insured while obtaining the policy.
The object of the Motor Vehicles Act is to protect innocent third-party victims of road traffic accidents.
In the present case, the petitioner is such a third-party victim and cannot be denied just compensation on account of internal disputes between the insurer and the insured.

39. Therefore, applying the principle of preponderance of probabilities and keeping in mind the beneficial object of the statute, this Tribunal is of the considered view that respondent No. 4 cannot escape from its statutory liability to indemnify the petitioner.

At the same time, liberty is reserved to the insurer to initiate independent proceedings against respondent No. 1, the owner of the offending vehicle, to recover the compensation amount if it is ultimately established that misrepresentation or fraud was indeed practiced at the time of obtaining the policy.
40. Accordingly, respondent No. 4 is held liable to satisfy the award in the first instance and pay compensation to the petitioner along with applicable interest.

Liberty is reserved to respondent No.
4 to recover the amount so paid from respondent No. 1 in accordance with law.

Insofar as respondent Nos. 2 and 3 are concerned, they appear to have been made as formal parties, and no material has been placed on record to show that they bear any liability to indemnify the owner.
Hence, the claim petition as against respondent Nos. 2 and 3 stands dismissed with the above observations.
I answer Issue No.2 partly in the affirmative.
41. ISSUE NO.3 :

In view of the above discussion, reasons stated and findings given to above issues,
I proceed to pass the following:
ORDER Claim Petition filed under Sec.166 of M.V.Act is partly allowed with cost.
Petition against the respondent No.2 and 3 is hereby dismissed.
Petitioner is awarded compensation of Rs.3,85,095/- together with interest @ 6% p.a. from the date of petition till the date of deposit with the Tribunal.
Kumar.

of the whole body, he did not specifically opine regarding the functional disability, i.e., the actual impact of the disability on the petitioner's earning capacity and day-to-day life.
It is a settled principle that medical disability and functional disability are not always identical.
Functional disability depends on the nature of occupation and the requirement of physical activity for earning livelihood.
As per record the petitioner was employed as a Delivery boy.
Having regard to the nature of the fracture, the subsequent removal of implants, the absence of any further surgical requirement,
and the fact that the petitioner is able to move independently though with certain restrictions, the medical assessment of 22% permanent disability of the limb appears to be on the higher side.
Therefore, while the medical assessment cannot be accepted in its entirety, the tribunal is of the opinion that a fair and reasonable estimate of functional disability of the petitioner, having regard to his avocation, would be taken at 8% of the whole body for the purpose of computing future loss of earning capacity and compensation.
In the absence of proof of income, this tribunal is of the opinion that the notional income to be assessed as per the guidelines of the Karnataka State Legal Service Authority.
In United India Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Kamalesh Singh [1995 ECJ 657], it was held that even where an agent's authority was disputed, the insurer remained liable to third parties but was free to recover from the agent.
Kumar.V. Alias Kumar Reddy vs Syed Aslam on 4 September, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/193894004/

37. In the present case, respondent No. 4 has not produced any cogent evidence to establish fraudulent intent on the part of the Respondent no 1 in relation to the policy.
The insurer has merely relied upon the discrepancy in the vehicle description, namely that the policy produced relates to a motorcycle, whereas the offending vehicle involved in the accident is a Tata Ace.
38. However, the legal position is well settled that the statutory liability of the insurer towards third-party victims under the Motor Vehicles Act cannot be avoided merely on the ground of misrepresentation or fraud practiced by the insured while obtaining the policy.
The object of the Motor Vehicles Act is to protect innocent third-party victims of road traffic accidents.
In the present case, the petitioner is such a third-party victim and cannot be denied just compensation on account of internal disputes between the insurer and the insured.
39. Therefore, applying the principle of preponderance of probabilities and keeping in mind the beneficial object of the statute, this Tribunal is of the considered view that respondent No. 4 cannot escape from its statutory liability to indemnify the petitioner.
At the same time, liberty is reserved to the insurer to initiate independent proceedings against respondent No. 1, the owner of the offending vehicle, to recover the compensation amount if it is ultimately established that misrepresentation or fraud was indeed practiced at the time of obtaining the policy.
